BBG's Simon White: nominal yields have in the main risen this year not because fiscal risks are expected to get even worse (or, equivalently, because inflation is about to become unanchored) - but because real growth is expected to rise

The economy's resilience can be seen in the chart below, showing that now none of the Fed's six regional manufacturing indices are in contraction. When all are rising, that has historically often coincided with a recession. That none are, shows that an imminent recession (say in 3-6 months) has quite a low probability.

The flipside of all this is that a magic level in yields is unlikely to trigger a durable and significant rally. Instead, we're not likely to see such a move until real growth or inflation are slowing.

Yardeni: Charlie Munger famously warned that there are three ways smart men can go broke: "Liquor, ladies, and leverage." NVIDIA co-founder and now former CEO Jensen Huang has run into trouble with the second of Munger's three L's. He won't go broke, but he is out of a good job.

Huang's departure rattled the AI trade, with NVIDIA shares plunging 4.3%, sending its forward P/E to 11.7 (charts). We promised you buying opportunities after the midterm elections. There were a bunch last Thursday and a few more [this week].

Our base case is that NVIDIA's financing strategy remains intact. Colette Kress, NVIDIA's longtime CFO and newly appointed interim CEO, has worked closely with Huang since 2013 and helped oversee the company's strategic investments and financing arrangements. During NVIDIA's August 26 earnings call, she defended these investments against accusations of circular financing, stating, "We recognize the scale of this support, and we know some will call it circular financing. We see it differently." She argued that these investments would generate attractive returns while strengthening NVIDIA's AI ecosystem, suggesting continuity under her leadership. We don't expect political constraints to meaningfully increase as a result of the controversy. Nor do we expect another trade conflict with China to erupt.

Even if some of the constraints intensify, they would likely turn existing speed bumps into bigger speed bumps rather than roadblocks to the AI investment boom. AI remains the latest evolution in the Digital Revolution that began with IBM's mainframes, and we expect the investment boom to continue without Huang (chart). We therefore view any resulting selloff as another buying opportunity for the AI trade.

Christophe Barraud (@C_Barraud) led his Top 10 Macro/Financial Charts of the Week with ZeroHedge’s “Bank of Nvidia” chart, which links to a detailed piece on the state of the Nvidia investing flywheel now that Jensen Huang is out and CFO Colette Kress is running Nvidia as interim CEO (while keeping the CFO job).

ZH’s argument: per the WSJ, Reuters and The Information, Kress was the one executive who kept asking what Nvidia’s guarantees were actually worth and, in at least one case, pushed back on how big they got.

That one case was the OpenAI Ohio backstop, which she cut from a reported $250B to the $105B that was eventually filed. ZH says that’s probably good for $NVDA shareholders but bad for the long list of AI companies counting on Nvidia’s balance sheet to fund 2027. Their bottom line: the circular AI funding machine “just lost its accelerator.”

Some numbers:

▪️ Nvidia’s 10-Q for the quarter ended Jul 26 showed $530.5B of commitments and guarantees, including $108.5B of guarantees and $36B of agreements to buy back capacity from AI cloud providers.

▪️ The next leg was supposed to be a $500B GPU financing platform that Huang launched in August with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman and KKR. The aim was to turn AI chips into collateral that lenders could fund, with Nvidia pledging to backstop up to 25% ($125B). Bloomberg reports it hasn’t closed a single deal in three months, partly because lenders want more than 25%, and Broadcom has been offering far more: it backstopped $30B of a $35B Anthropic TPU deal (86%) and $43B of a second $63B deal (about 68%). If Nvidia wouldn’t offer more under Huang, it seems unlikely it will under Kress.

▪️ Existing deals should survive, though. Goldman’s James Schneider expects every announced commitment to be honored. The next round of deals is what gets harder, he says.

The fallout from an Nvidia pullback in financing:

▪️ UBS’s Tim Arcuri estimates Nvidia generates about $50 - 60B of free cash flow a quarter, much of it recycled back into the AI ecosystem. For scale, the 10-Q IOUs alone already equal roughly 9-11 quarters of that FCF.

▪️ Investment-grade corporate spreads are just 0.89%, near the tightest since at least 2013, while the ICE BofA CCC & Lower spread hit 13.56% on Oct 23, its widest since summer 2020 and above even the 2022 peak. Most of Nvidia’s borrowers sit somewhere between those two extremes, and Nvidia’s guarantee is what turns debt backed by a cash-burning AI lab or a junk-rated neocloud into an investment-grade loan. Take it away and some deals just get more expensive, while others may not get done at all. CoreWeave fell 11% on news of Huang’s exit on the same day it was marketing a $4B+ investment-grade loan where Nvidia is presumably the guarantor.

We probably won’t learn much from Nvidia’s Q3 earnings call on Tuesday (Nov 17). Kress has been in the job less than a week, and a CFO-turned-interim-CEO with a board search underway has every reason to say “existing commitments will be honored” and nothing more.

The more useful read will come from the Q3 10-Q, which updates the footnotes behind that $530.5B for the quarter ended in late October. According to the WSJ, that’s the stretch when Nvidia was already pulling back. In late August it paused some of its credit-support deals with cloud providers (guarantees given in exchange for a cut of their revenue) and started requiring executive-team and board sign-off on each one. By October, the WSJ reports, it had begun turning off the tap. If guarantees and cloud buy-back commitments flattened or fell from July’s $108.5B and $36B, the “Bank of Nvidia” was already cutting back even before Huang left.
